sense: if …: I would go if I could

terms.gloss: I would do it if I could (but I can’t)
terms.grammar: the imperfect subjunctive in both clauses: unreal in the present
evidence: Publil. Sent. Q 83: Quis miserum scīret, verba nisi habēret dolor?
terms.comment: For what is not so now. The two clauses may differ in time: quō tē modō accēpissem, nisi īrātus essem!, how I would have treated you, if I were not angry (Cic. Tusc. 4.78).

terms.gloss: I would have done it if I had been able
terms.grammar: the pluperfect subjunctive in both clauses: unreal in the past
evidence: Cic. Sen. 11: nisi tū āmīsissēs, numquam recēpissem

terms.gloss: I would (should) do it if I could (imagined)
terms.grammar: the present subjunctive in both clauses: a supposition
evidence: Publil. Sent. N 2: Nīl peccent oculī, sī animus oculīs imperet.
terms.comment: For what may yet be, only supposed. So the polite velim, “I’d like” (see want).

terms.gloss: would, in reported speech: he said he would …
terms.grammar: the future infinitive in an accusative and infinitive
terms.comment: After a verb of saying or thinking, English “would” of the future is the future infinitive, its participle agreeing with the subject; esse is often left out.

phrases.latin: Quis miserum scīret, verba nisi habēret dolor?
phrases.english: Who would know a man was unhappy, if pain had no words?

phrases.latin: quō tē modō, inquit, accēpissem, nisi īrātus essem!
phrases.english: “How I would have treated you,” he said, “if I weren’t angry!”

phrases.latin: 'certē,' inquit rīdēns, 'nam nisi tū āmīsissēs, numquam recēpissem'
phrases.english: “Certainly,” he said, laughing, “for if you hadn’t lost it, I would never have taken it back.”

phrases.latin: Nīl peccent oculī, sī animus oculīs imperet.
phrases.english: The eyes would do no wrong, if the mind ruled them.

phrases.latin: sī mihi Nausicaa patriōs concēderet hortōs, Alcinoō possem dīcere "mālō meōs"
phrases.english: if Nausicaa offered me her father’s gardens, I could say to Alcinous, “I prefer my own”

phrases.latin: sē impetum hostium, quantum corpore ūnō posset obsistī, exceptūrum
phrases.english: (he said) that he would take the enemy’s charge himself, as far as one body could hold it
